chapter_title: Firewall Management with nftables and Advanced SELinux Networking

screens.title: Firewall Management with nftables and Advanced SELinux Networking
screens.subtitle: Unify packet filtering, NAT, and process-level network controls on RHEL using nftables and SELinux

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn why nftables replaces the older iptables family and how SELinux complements packet filtering by controlling which processes may use network resources. We will focus on practical skills: writing rulesets with tables, chains, sets and maps; implementing NAT and port forwarding; and labeling ports and adjusting booleans so services like Apache can operate without being blocked by mandatory access control. You will see concrete configuration examples for a typical web server architecture with an external interface and an internal subnet, and a hands-on scenario that combines port forwarding and masquerading with SELinux adjustments. Along the way we'll cover common mistakes — like forgetting to flush old rules or mislabeling ports — and how to verify what the kernel is actually doing using the nft commands and audit logs. By the end you should be able to write a clear, persistent nftables ruleset, use sets and maps for efficiency, and diagnose SELinux denials that affect network services. Consider how atomic ruleset updates and unified address-family tables make firewall management simpler in hybrid IPv4/IPv6 cloud deployments.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: nftables provides a unified, efficient firewall framework; SELinux enforces which processes may use ports and sockets. Together they provide layered network security on RHEL.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide hands-on mastery of nftables and SELinux for networked services. First, you will understand nftables architecture and how it improves on the older iptables family through a unified framework and more expressive primitives. Second, you will be able to author rulesets using tables, chains, hooks, and policy defaults, and you will use the inet table to handle both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic. Third, you will design and use sets and maps to manage large address or port lists efficiently and reduce kernel overhead. Fourth, you will implement NAT, port forwarding, and connection tracking so that services on internal networks can communicate through an external interface. Each objective pairs a practical skill with the reason it matters in production: clarity, performance, and secure process-level control. For example, using sets reduces duplicated rules and makes updates atomic, which matters in dynamic cloud environments. As you progress, aim to verify each competency by loading a ruleset, confirming it with the nft list ruleset command, and checking SELinux audit logs when a service behaves unexpectedly.

keyIdea.text: Focus on ruleset structure, efficient matching with sets and maps, NAT mechanics, and SELinux port and boolean configuration.

narration.text: Continuing your competency path, these objectives emphasize process-level controls and diagnostics. First, you will be able to integrate SELinux network contexts with nftables rules so that allowed traffic reaches the intended processes. That includes managing port contexts with semanage and enabling booleans such as allowing a web server to connect to a remote database. Second, you will learn to troubleshoot nftables and SELinux interactions by using nft list ruleset, nft monitor, journalctl for the nftables service, and audit tools for SELinux denials. Fourth, you will avoid risky shortcuts such as disabling SELinux; instead you will learn to adjust policy or ports to resolve denials. screens.title: Why nftables replaces iptables
screens.subtitle: Unified framework, atomic updates, and expressive matching

narration.text: nftables is the modern replacement for the iptables family because it provides a single, unified command and kernel infrastructure for packet filtering and NAT across address families. Where iptables required separate utilities and modules for IPv4, IPv6, ARP and bridging, nftables supports ip, ip6, arp and bridge tables and also introduces the inet table to handle IPv4 and IPv6 together. This matters because mixed stack servers and cloud environments frequently see both protocols in play. Another core advantage is atomic ruleset updates: you prepare a complete ruleset and load it in one step, avoiding inconsistent partial states that can occur with sequential rule insertions. nftables also introduces sets and maps which let you group many addresses or map inputs to outputs so the kernel can match efficiently. A practical example: instead of many repeated rules to allow each admin IP for SSH, you define a set and write one rule that references it. A common misconception is to treat nftables as just syntactic sugar; in practice its kernel-side improvements and object types yield measurable manageability and performance gains. Takeaway: move complex, dynamic policies to nftables sets and atomically deploy them to reduce configuration drift and errors.

keyIdea.title: Migration rationale
keyIdea.text: Use nftables when you need unified address-family handling, atomic updates, and efficient large-list matching with sets and maps.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Why nftables
Comparison
Unified framework
Handles IPv4, IPv6, ARP and bridging from the same tool; use inet tables to cover both IP families.
Atomic ruleset updates
Load a complete ruleset in one operation to avoid transient inconsistent states during updates.
Sets and maps
Group addresses or map inputs to outputs for concise, efficient kernel matching.
Example
Instead of adding many separate allow rules for management hosts, define a set of admin IPs and write a single accept rule that references it. This reduces complexity and eases updates.
Common misconception
People sometimes assume nftables is purely syntactic sugar over iptables. In truth it changes kernel matching primitives and provides objects like sets and maps that reduce rule duplication and improve performance. Treat it as a more capable, modern framework rather than a drop-in re-skin.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Prefer nftables for modern deployments for unified handling of address families, atomic loading, and efficient large-list matching.

screens.title: Core nftables building blocks
screens.subtitle: Tables, Chains, Hooks and Policies explained

narration.text: At the heart of nftables are a small number of composable concepts you will use in every ruleset: tables, chains, hooks, and rules. A table is simply a container that groups chains; tables are typed by address family such as ip, ip6, inet, arp or bridge. A chain is an ordered list of rules and is attached to a hook — a predefined point in the network stack like input, forward, prerouting, or postrouting. The chain type and hook determine when packets are evaluated and whether the chain is suitable for filtering or NAT. For example, a chain attached to the input hook processes packets destined to local processes, while a postrouting hook is used for NAT after routing decisions. Chains also have a policy: accept or drop as a default action when no rule matches. Understanding these relationships is crucial when you design where a rule must live. A typical pattern is an inet table with input, forward and output chains and a separate ip table with a nat table containing prerouting and postrouting chains for DNAT and masquerade. Misconfiguring a hook or using the wrong priority can leave packets unhandled or break NAT. The core claim: place each rule in the chain that matches where packets are processed in the stack.

keyIdea.title: Structure matters
keyIdea.text: Put filtering rules on appropriate hooks and use table types to match the address families you need to protect.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Core Blocks
Architecture
Table
Container typed by address family. Use inet for dual-stack handling.
Chain
Ordered rules attached to a hook with a policy. Example chains: input, forward, output.
Hook
Predefined processing points in the network stack where chains run, such as prerouting or postrouting for NAT.
Practical guidance
  • Use input hook for packets destined to local services and set a restrictive default policy there.
  • Use prerouting for DNAT before routing decisions; use postrouting for masquerade after routing.
  • Choose inet tables when you need identical rules for IPv4 and IPv6 to avoid duplication.
  • Set policy explicitly to avoid accidental openness from implicit defaults.
Example rule placement
Put accept rules for established connections in input chain and DNAT actions in the nat prerouting chain to ensure correct packet transformation order.

screens.title: Basic webserver nftables ruleset
screens.subtitle: A concrete ruleset for SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS with a drop policy

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete nftables file for a web server. The example is structured as an inet table named filter with input, forward and output chains. The input chain sets a default drop policy, allows loopback, accepts established and related connection states, and then permits SSH, HTTP and HTTPS by destination port. This pattern is common on single-host web servers where minimal exposure is required. Loading such a file atomically applies all statements and avoids partial state. A practical walkthrough: flush ruleset clears previous rules so you start clean. The input chain entries first accept loopback to keep local tools functioning, then accept connection-tracked established traffic to keep return packets flowing, and finally accept specific TCP destination ports. Note the explicit accept rules make intent clear and the policy drop complements them by preventing any other inbound access. When you test, load the file with nft -f and verify with nft list ruleset. A common pitfall is editing a file and not reloading it, or forgetting to persist it for reboots. Always validate from a console path before saving to production to avoid locking yourself out.

keyIdea.title: Safe default
keyIdea.text: Use policy drop with explicit accepts and rely on connection tracking for return traffic.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Webserver ruleset
Ruleset (example)
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

        # Allow loopback traffic
        iif "lo" accept

        # Allow established and related connections
        ct state { established, related } accept

        # Allow SSH (port 22)
        tcp dport 22 accept

        # Allow HTTP (port 80)
        tcp dport 80 accept

        # Allow HTTPS (port 443)
        tcp dport 443 accept
    }

    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
    }

    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
    }
}
Explanation & checks
  • flush ruleset resets the kernel state so the file applies cleanly.
  • ct state established, related lets return traffic through without per-connection allows.
  • Using policy drop makes explicit accepts the only way in; avoids accidental openness.
  • After loading, run nft list ruleset and confirm SSH remains available before closing session.
Common-mistake
Forgetting to leave a console session open while testing can lock you out. Always test with a recovery path.

screens.title: Sets and Maps
screens.subtitle: Grouping and mapping values for efficient matching

narration.text: Sets and maps are two powerful nftables features that reduce duplication and accelerate kernel matching. A set is a collection of values such as IP addresses, ranges, or ports. You define a set once and then reference it in rules, which lets a single rule cover many elements. A practical example from the chapter is grouping administration IPs into a set and writing one SSH accept rule against that set. Maps extend the idea by mapping an input value to an output value — for example mapping source IP to a target port or verdict for dynamic handling. A map can be used in NAT scenarios or complex routing decisions without long chains of conditional rules. When creating sets remember to choose the correct type, for example ipv4_addr for IPv4 addresses and include flags like interval when you want ranges. A common misconception is that sets are only for convenience; they are actually more efficient because the kernel handles membership tests faster than repeated individual rules. The takeaway: prefer sets and maps for any large or frequently changing list of addresses or ports to keep rules concise, readable and performant.

keyIdea.title: Efficient matching
keyIdea.text: Use sets for many values and maps when you must transform values; both reduce rule duplication and improve kernel performance.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Sets & Maps
Set example
# Define a set of admin IPs
set admin_ips {
    type ipv4_addr;
    flags interval;
    elements = { 192.168.1.10, 192.168.1.20-192.168.1.30 }
}

# Use the set in a rule
chain input {
    ip saddr @admin_ips tcp dport 22 accept
}
Maps and use cases
- Maps translate input to output values and are useful for dynamic NAT or routing decisions.
- Use maps when you need to change a packet field based on source or another key without many conditional rules.
- Verify types: selecting ipv4_addr or inet_service matters for accurate matches and to avoid load-time errors.
Pro tip
When you update a large set, prefer preparing a new set definition and atomically reloading the ruleset so kernel membership changes take effect without transient mismatches.

screens.title: NAT: Masquerade and Port Forwarding
screens.subtitle: How to implement SNAT and DNAT for internal services

narration.text: Network Address Translation in nftables is handled through tables and chains of type nat attached to prerouting or postrouting hooks. For outbound address translation from an internal network, masquerade in postrouting changes the source of packets to the firewall's external IP so replies route correctly. For inbound port forwarding, use DNAT in the prerouting chain to rewrite the destination IP and port to an internal host before routing. The chapter includes practical code samples: a postrouting rule that masquerades traffic from 192.168.0.0/24 when leaving via eth0, and a prerouting DNAT that forwards TCP port 80 on the external interface to an internal web server. Note that for NAT to work you must enable IP forwarding on the kernel and ensure forward chains accept the forwarded traffic when appropriate. Common mistakes include missing ip_forward or forgetting to allow forwarded packets with connection tracking. Always test DNAT by initiating a connection from an external host and verify the packet path with nft monitor, and remember persistence: load the rules and add them to the system's nftables configuration so they survive restarts. The key idea: prerouting changes destination, postrouting changes source.

keyIdea.title: NAT roles
keyIdea.text: Use prerouting for DNAT (incoming destination changes) and postrouting for SNAT/masquerade (outgoing source changes).

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › NAT & Port Forwarding
Masquerade example
table ip nat {
    chain postrouting {
        type nat hook postrouting priority 100; policy accept;
        oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.0.0/24 masquerade
    }
}
Enable IP forwarding to allow NATed packets to traverse: set net.ipv4.ip_forward to one and persist it. Confirm the firewall accepts forwarded connections in the forward chain.
Port forward (DNAT)
table ip nat {
    chain prerouting {
        type nat hook prerouting priority -100; policy accept;
        iifname "eth0" tcp dport 80 dnat to 192.168.0.10:80
    }
}
Test DNAT from an external client and check that forwarding allows the translated packet to reach the internal server. Use nft monitor for live packet events if you need to debug.

screens.title: Load, persist and verify your ruleset
screens.subtitle: Safe deployment practices and common pitfalls

narration.text: Applying and persisting nftables rulesets must be done carefully to avoid accidental lockouts or inconsistent firewall states. The common workflow is to author a complete file, test it locally with nft -f to load it atomically, and then verify current state with nft list ruleset. For persistence, systems often use /etc/sysconfig/nftables. conf or a systemd unit that loads your chosen file. If your distribution's nftables. service expects a different path, copy your tested file into that location or create a systemd drop-in that points to your file. Key safety checks: always keep a recovery path such as an open console or a timed rollback, and prefer policy drop with explicit allows so you can reason about exposures. Common mistakes include forgetting to flush ruleset and creating duplicates, or editing an on-disk file without reloading the kernel state. Diagnosing load errors often involves journalctl -u nftables. service for syntax or type issues, and nft monitor to observe real-time matches. Finally, document the interface names and network ranges used in rules to avoid accidental misapplication when interfaces change. The core advice: test atomically, verify, persist intentionally, and prepare a fallback.

keyIdea.title: Safe deployment
keyIdea.text: Test rulesets atomically, verify active state, and ensure persistence with the distribution's nftables configuration to avoid surprises on reboot.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Load & Persist
Deployment checklist
  1. Create and save a complete ruleset file and include flush ruleset at top so previous state is cleared.
  2. Load the file with nft -f and confirm no syntax errors.
  3. Verify active rules with nft list ruleset and test connectivity from a safe client.
  4. Persist by copying to /etc/sysconfig/nftables.conf or configuring nftables.service to load your file, then enable the service.
Troubleshooting tips
  • Use journalctl -u nftables.service to find load-time errors when the service starts.
  • Use nft monitor to see how packets match rules in real time while you test.
  • Avoid in-place edits without reload; always reload the tested file so the kernel matches your intended configuration.
  • Keep a rescue console or scheduled rollback to prevent lockout during remote changes.

screens.title: Inspecting nftables activity and errors
screens.subtitle: nft list ruleset, nft monitor and service logs

narration.text: Diagnosing firewall behavior requires both static inspection and live observation. nft list ruleset shows the current active configuration in the kernel so you can confirm what was loaded. nft monitor is a live tool that prints packet events and can show which rule a packet matched or why it was dropped. For load-time or runtime errors related to nftables service management, journalctl -u nftables. service is your first stop. When you make a change and see unexpected behavior, first confirm the active ruleset, then use nft monitor from a test client while recreating the traffic. This will reveal whether packets are reaching the kernel and which rule is affecting them. If a ruleset fails to load, journalctl usually includes the line number or the reason such as a type mismatch in a set definition. A common troubleshooting flow: verify file syntax, load it in a non-production test environment, run nft -f, then monitor with nft monitor while exercising the traffic. Keep in mind that some drops are intentional due to policy defaults; logs and monitor output help you distinguish intentional policy from misconfiguration.

keyIdea.title: Observe & verify
keyIdea.text: Use nft list ruleset for state, nft monitor for live matches, and journalctl for service load errors to diagnose firewall issues.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Inspect & Monitor
Useful commands
- nft list ruleset — show active kernel ruleset.
- nft monitor — observe packet matching and verdicts in real time.
- journalctl -u nftables.service — review load-time errors and service logs.
Check example
If a rule appears present but packets are still dropped, monitor traffic while you attempt a connection to see whether the packet matches a different chain, or whether connection tracking classifies it as invalid.
Live debugging
  1. Confirm ruleset with nft list ruleset.
  2. Start nft monitor and recreate the traffic from a test client.
  3. Interpret monitor output to find matching rule or drop reason.
  4. Check journalctl if a ruleset failed to load or a service reports errors.

screens.title: SELinux network concepts
screens.subtitle: Ports, network interface contexts and booleans

narration.text: SELinux is a mandatory access control system that governs what processes can do, including which ports they may bind and which network resources they may access. Port contexts label ports with types such as http_port_t for HTTP services. If a process attempts to bind to a non-standard port, SELinux will deny it unless you add an appropriate semanage port mapping. Network interface contexts are another label category, though they are used less frequently in typical server hardening. SELinux booleans provide on/off switches for common behaviors; for example enabling a boolean that allows the httpd process to initiate network connections to a remote database. Use setsebool with the persistent flag to keep changes across reboots. Troubleshooting SELinux networking involves examining the audit log for AVC denials and using sealert to get human-readable advice. A common mistake is to disable SELinux entirely when a denial happens; the safer approach is to adjust ports or booleans, or in complex cases create a local policy module after careful analysis. The key claim: SELinux controls process permissions while nftables controls packet flow; both must be aligned for services to function securely.

keyIdea.title: Process-level control
keyIdea.text: Use semanage to set port labels and setsebool to enable required behaviors rather than disabling SELinux.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › SELinux Networking
Port contexts
- Use semanage port to add a non-standard port to a service context so the process can bind.
- Example command to label a port for httpd is provided in the chapter as a demonstration command.
Booleans
Enable booleans like httpd_can_network_connect_db with setsebool -P to allow httpd to contact remote databases persistently.
Troubleshooting SELinux
  • Search AVC denials with ausearch -m AVC or use sealert -a to get suggestions.
  • Avoid disabling SELinux; prefer targeted semanage port additions or enabling booleans.
  • Back up policy modules before making custom changes to preserve recoverability.

screens.title: Practical lab: Web server with NAT and SELinux
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step plan to implement the chapter's scenario

narration.text: This hands-on scenario ties the chapter's concepts together. You're configuring a RHEL web server with eth0 external and eth1 internal where an internal host serves web traffic. Steps: define a management subnet set to permit SSH only from 192.168.10.0/24, create an inet filter table with input chain policy drop, allow established traffic and loopback, accept SSH from the management set, and accept HTTP/HTTPS from anywhere. Next, create an ip nat table with a prerouting chain to DNAT port 80 on eth0 to the internal web server IP, and a postrouting masquerade rule to change outbound source addresses to the firewall's external IP for the internal network. Enable net. ipv4. ip_forward so NAT can forward traffic at the kernel level. For SELinux, if the web server uses standard ports no port relabeling is needed, but enable the boolean that lets httpd connect to databases if the application needs it. After the changes, load the file atomically, verify nft list ruleset, test connectivity, and check audit logs if any denial occurs. If you see a denial, use ausearch and sealert to find the suggested semanage or setsebool commands. This scenario practises safe deployment, NAT, and SELinux adjustments in concert.

keyIdea.title: Integrated setup
keyIdea.text: Combine sets, nat, and SELinux booleans to allow access from intended networks while preserving process-level constraints.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Hands-on Scenario
Starter rules and commands
# Define management subnet
define management_subnet = { 192.168.10.0/24 }

table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
        iif "lo" accept
        ct state { established, related } accept
        ip saddr $management_subnet tcp dport 22 accept
        tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
    }
}

table ip nat {
    chain prerouting {
        type nat hook prerouting priority -100; policy accept;
        iifname "eth0" tcp dport 80 dnat to 192.168.50.100:80
    }

    chain postrouting {
        type nat hook postrouting priority 100; policy accept;
        oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.50.0/24 masquerade
    }
}
Verification and SELinux steps
- Load the file with nft -f and check nft list ruleset for the expected tables and chains.
- Enable IP forwarding: set net.ipv4.ip_forward to one and persist it in /etc/sysctl.d.
- If using standard ports no semanage change is needed. To add a non-standard port, use semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080.
- Turn on httpd network database access with setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on when required.
Final check
Key Takeaway

Test and verify traffic paths, SELinux contexts, and persistence before declaring the deployment complete.

screens.title: Diagnosing SELinux-related network failures
screens.subtitle: From audit logs to semanage fixes

narration.text: When a network service is blocked even though nftables allows traffic, SELinux is often the missing piece. The hallmark symptom is connection refused or denial messages in audit logs. Start troubleshooting by searching for AVC denials using ausearch or by running sealert -a on the audit log for a digest and suggested fixes. Typical causes include a service attempting to bind to a non-standard port without an appropriate port context or a denied network connection because a required boolean is off. For port issues, semanage port -a -t with the appropriate type resolves binding denials; for network connectivity needs, setsebool -P toggles persistent behavior such as allowing httpd to connect to network databases. A misconception is that all network denials are firewall-related; always check audit logs when services misbehave. The safe resolution path is: reproduce the failure, collect AVC denials, use sealert recommendations, and apply semanage or setsebool changes rather than disabling SELinux. After changes, test again and archive the policy modification steps for operational records. The core lesson: use audit evidence to guide specific SELinux adjustments. Diagnosing SELinux-related network failures means use audit logs and sealert to identify selinux denials and apply targeted semanage or setsebool adjustments rather than disabling selinux.. In practical terms, from audit logs to semanage fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Evidence-driven fixes
keyIdea.text: Use audit logs and sealert to identify SELinux denials and apply targeted semanage or setsebool adjustments rather than disabling SELinux.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › SELinux Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting flow
  1. Reproduce the failure so logs contain the denial.
  2. Search AVC denials with ausearch -m AVC -ts today or run sealert -a for guidance.
  3. Apply targeted fixes such as semanage port additions or persistent setsebool toggles.
  4. Retest and document changes; do not disable SELinux as a shortcut.
Concrete commands
- Check for denials: sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts today
- Human readable analysis: sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log
- Add port mapping: sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080
- Enable boolean persistently: sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on
Common pitfall
Do not suppress audit logs or disable SELinux to make problems disappear; use the logs as your guide to the minimal corrective change.

narration.text: These concise concept cards recap the most important nftables ideas. First, nftables itself is the modern packet filtering framework that unifies previous separate tools for different address families, and it should be your primary firewall tool on RHEL. Second, a table is simply a container for chains and is typed by address family; use the inet table when you need rules that apply to both IPv4 and IPv6. Third, a chain is an ordered list of rules attached to a hook and carrying a default policy; choosing the right hook determines when packets are inspected and whether a rule affects NAT or local delivery. Remember these building blocks so you can design clear rulesets and avoid placing rules in the wrong processing stage. Key Concepts — Part 1 means tables, chains and hooks define where and when packets are processed: get this right before adding complex rules.. In practical terms, essential nftables building blocks. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Foundations
keyIdea.text: Tables, chains and hooks define where and when packets are processed: get this right before adding complex rules.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Key Concepts
nftables
The modern unified packet filtering framework replacing the iptables family.
Table
Container for chains, typed by address family such as ip, ip6, or inet for dual-stack rules.
Chain & Hook
A chain is an ordered rule list attached to a hook like input or postrouting which determines when it runs.
Summary

Design rulesets by selecting the correct table type and hook, then use explicit accepts with a restrictive policy to reduce accidental exposure.

narration.text: These final cards summarize sets and maps, NAT roles, and SELinux networking essentials. First, sets and maps let you express large or dynamic lists concisely while improving kernel matching performance. Second, NAT uses prerouting for destination translation and postrouting for source translation; DNAT forwards inbound requests to internal hosts and masquerade hides internal source addresses for outbound traffic. Third, SELinux enforces which processes may bind ports and initiate network connections; fix denials with semanage and setsebool rather than disabling SELinux. Together, these concepts form a layered approach: nftables controls packet paths, and SELinux controls process permissions. When both are configured correctly, network services operate both reachably and securely. As you finish this chapter, ask yourself which audit evidence to check first when a service doesn't respond — the active ruleset or the SELinux audit log — and then follow the targeted troubleshooting path shown earlier.

keyIdea.title: Layered defense
keyIdea.text: Use nftables for packet-level control, sets/maps for efficiency, NAT for translation, and SELinux for process-level permissions.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Key Concepts
Sets & Maps
Group addresses or map inputs to outputs to reduce rule duplication and improve performance.
NAT, MASQ, DNAT
Use prerouting for DNAT and postrouting for masquerade to forward and hide addresses respectively.
SELinux Networking
Label ports with semanage and enable booleans with setsebool -P instead of disabling SELinux.
Final takeaway

Combine nftables object-oriented rules with SELinux process controls to implement secure and maintainable network policies on RHEL.
